scenes.name: Funk industrial
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Tras la caída de P-Funk, muchos ritmos nuevos vinieron de fuera: Kraftwerk, Art of Noise («Beat Box», «Close (to the Edit)»), Talking Heads (Stop Making Sense, con Bernie Worrell) y el «Genius of Love» de Tom Tom Club. Herbie Hancock pidió a su mánager Tony Meilandt unos temas de hip hop y con Bill Laswell y Grandmixer D.S.T. hizo «Rockit» (Future Shock, 1983): la cima del funk industrial nada más empezar. Laswell (Material, Time Zone con John Lydon, Manu Dibango, los Last Poets) dejó su sello de bajo grueso; sellos como Celluloid, On-U Sound, Tommy Boy o Def Jam sacaban ritmos ásperos de raspados metálicos y tensión de Guerra Fría. On-U Sound de Adrian Sherwood fichó a la sección rítmica de Sugarhill (Doug Wimbish, Skip McDonald, Keith LeBlanc): Tackhead, el «No Sell Out» con la voz de Malcolm X, «el P-Funk de los ochenta» según Pedro Bell.
scenes.family: Hip hop, go-go y funk de los noventa

scenes.name: Public Image Ltd.
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Tras la implosión de los Sex Pistols en Winterland (enero de 1978), John Lydon recupera su nombre y monta con Jah Wobble y Keith Levene «el conjunto arquetípico del postpunk»: no una banda sino una «compañía de comunicaciones», sin manager, en traje y con el reggae como único punto en común («los tres éramos fanáticos enfermos del dub»). El bajo dub de Wobble es el latido humano; la guitarra de Levene, «el Jimi Hendrix del postpunk», queda libre para perder la compostura. Public Image (1978) todavía rockea, pero «Fodderstompf», broma disco de casi ocho minutos, anuncia el estudio-como-instrumento de Metal Box. Lydon declara que la única música contemporánea que le interesa es la disco y compara el rock con «una iglesia, una religión, una farsa».
scenes.family: Vanguardia postpunk: dub, funk y política

podcast.title: Sex Pistols Audition (1975)
podcast.body: In 1975, Johnny Rotten was considered for the lead singer position of the Sex Pistols after walking into Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop. His distinctive appearance, specifically wearing an "I Hate Pink Floyd" t-shirt, immediately caught attention and played a role in his consideration for the band. "Johnny Rotten walked into Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop in 1975. He was immediately considered for the job of lead singer of the sex pistols, based on the fact that he was wearing an eye-hate pink Floyd t-shirt."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 15

podcast.title: Eclectic Musical Tastes Revealed (1977)
podcast.body: In 1977, shortly after the Sex Pistols released "God Save the Queen," John Lydon was interviewed by a London radio station to play his favorite songs on a special program called "The Punk and His Music." While everyone expected the wildest punk, he, the supposed "Antichrist of punk," played reggae, Krautrock bands like Can, Tim Buckley ballads, and Captain Beefheart's wild hip-hop experimentation. This music, despised by the punk scene at the time, later became a significant reference for post-punk. "Todo el mundo esperaba escuchar el punk más albaje, pero en su lugar, el supuesto anticristo del punk, un setem más de Rigi, de bandas de Krauro como Cannes, Valadas de Tim Buckley, o la loquísima experimentación hip-hid de Captain Vithhart."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La traición que salvó al punk. PiL

podcast.title: Decision to End Johnny Rotten Persona (January 14, 1978)
podcast.body: John Lydon, previously known as Johnny Rotten and the primary face of punk, decided to "kill his character" at the Sex Pistols' last concert of their American tour, which also became their final show together. He was reportedly tired of playing the same accelerated three-chord Chuck Berry style and felt music could be more. "Los expuestos, la banda más grande del momento, acababa de perder a su vocalista."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La traición que salvó al punk. PiL

podcast.title: Missed Pan Am Flight 103 (1988)
podcast.body: Johnny Lydon and his wife, Nora, narrowly missed Pan Am Flight 103 on December 21, 1988, which was later bombed over Lockerbie, Scotland. Delays caused by Nora taking too long to pack, a subsequent argument, and getting stuck in traffic on the way to Heathrow Airport meant they missed the flight by minutes, thus saving their lives. "Nora, his wife, took too long to pack. They had a big fight, which delayed them even more, and then they got stuck in traffic on the way to Heathrow. They missed their flight by minutes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Airplanes!

podcast.title: Near-Miss Lockerbie Bombing (1988)
podcast.body: John Lydon, of the Sex Pistols and Public Image Limited, came very close to dying in the bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, on December 21, 1988. He and his wife, Nora, had seats on the flight but missed it by minutes due to his wife taking too long to pack, which caused a big fight, and then getting stuck in traffic on the way to Heathrow Airport. "Johnny Leiden with public image limited and death disco. He came very, very close to dying in the Lockerbie bombing in December of 1988."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Airplanes!

podcast.title: Aggressive Dance Punk with Public Image Limited
podcast.body: After his time with the Sex Pistols, Johnny Lydon led Public Image Limited (PIL) in exploring a more aggressive form of dance punk. While still danceable, PIL's music had a distinct edge, described as "scary," "agitated," and "twitchy." "There was also a more aggressive version of this approach, led by Johnny Lydon's post-sex pistols band Public Image Limited."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

podcast.title: Auditioning Michael Balzary (Flea) for PiL
podcast.body: In 1984, Johnny Lydon auditioned a young bass player from Los Angeles named Michael Balzary (later known as Flea) for Public Image Limited. Flea got the gig but chose instead to stick with his new band, the Red Hot Chili Peppers, which he was forming with his friend Anthony. "One of the people, Johnny auditioned for the band in 1984, was a young bass player from Los Angeles named Michael Ballzary."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: Belief in No Future (Pre-Metal Box)
podcast.body: Prior to *Metal Box*, Johnny Rotten famously chanted that there was "no future," reflecting the punk ethos. However, the subsequent release of *Metal Box* demonstrated that there was indeed a significant future for music, proving his earlier statement wrong. "Johnny Rote encantaba que no había futuro, pero como hemos visto, había mucho futuro, y poco después lo demostró con Metalbox."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La traición que salvó al punk. PiL

podcast.title: Caregiver for Wife with Alzheimer's
podcast.body: Johnny Lydon is a dedicated caregiver for his wife, Nora, whom he affectionately calls "babby," as she battles Alzheimer's disease. His personal experience with childhood memory loss from meningitis allows him to deeply empathize with her condition and the challenges she faces, providing her with round-the-clock care. "He will also tell you about his wife Nora who he's caring for as she deals with Alzheimer's."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians Battling Disease Part 2

podcast.title: Childhood Meningitis
podcast.body: As a child, Johnny Lydon contracted a severe case of meningitis that left him in a coma for nearly a year. The lasting effects of this illness are credited with causing his distinctive stare. "Johnny Liden, who came down with a terrible case of meningitis as a kid, which left him comatose for nearly a year. The after effects give him that distinctive stare."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Health Issues of Musicians

podcast.title: Critique of Punk Music (Metal Box Era)
podcast.body: John Lydon contended that punk, despite its revolutionary origins, had become "something fascist." He championed Public Image Ltd as an entity that broke away from such limitations. "decía que el punk, en su origen, género revolucionario, se había convertido en algo fascista."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La traición que salvó al punk. PiL

podcast.title: Dark Music Contribution
podcast.body: Johnny Lydon's work with Public Image Limited was noted for its dark sound, contributing to the development of the Goth scene. "Johnny Lydon's public image limited was pretty dark, same with Killing Joke."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Good Goth - Part 1

podcast.title: Declined Plastic Beach Participation
podcast.body: John Lydon was approached to contribute to the Gorillaz album "Plastic Beach" but declined, stating he had "better things to do." "Then again, Johnny Liden and Tom Weitz also said they had better things to do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Gorillaz - A History

podcast.title: Fan of Trout Mask Replica
podcast.body: The future Johnny Rotten of the Sex Pistols was among the many individuals who bought and listened to Captain Beefheart's "Trout Mask Replica," specifically because of its "un-listenable" and challenging nature. "But many people, like the future Johnny Rotten of the Sex Bistels, bought it and played it because it was un-listenable."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1

podcast.title: First Major Chart Hit
podcast.body: Johnny Rotten, formerly of the Sex Pistols, was one of the "forefathers of punk, art rock, and new wave" who secured his first major hit song ever on a Billboard chart via the Modern Rock Chart in the late 1980s. "former sex pistol Johnny Rotten."

podcast.title: No Biological Children
podcast.body: Johnny Rotten and his wife Nora never had any biological children together. "Johnny and his wife Nora never had any kids together."

podcast.title: Nora's Age
podcast.body: Nora is described as "quite a bit older than John." "Johnny met mom through Ari. Johnny married mom. And yes, she's quite a bit older than John."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Star Kids ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Outrage over "Aggressive Bubblegum" Comment
podcast.body: John Lydon, also known as Johnny Rotten, the lead singer of the Sex Pistols, expressed extreme anger at Tom Verlaine's comment that punk music was merely "slightly aggressive Bubblegum." Lydon interpreted this as a jealous and superficial insult, accusing Verlaine and his "New York trendy expletive" peers of being "posers" from wealthy families who couldn't comprehend the "ferocious and frontline" content of the Sex Pistols. "No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, again I've always hated the label punk But if he calls the Sex Pistols slightly aggressive Bubblegum, then he really is showing what a jealous, superficial, expletive, I always thought he was, okay I didn't say expletive, the newspaper said that Johnny goes on to say, and he is part and parcel now he's talking about Tom Verlaine Him and all of them New York trendy expletives that had the liberty to call themselves punk They weren't really, they were posers."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s
srcs.episode: Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music

srcs.episode: Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music

podcast.title: PiL Influenced by Can
podcast.body: His post-Sex Pistols band, PiL, was clearly influenced by Can's distinctive groovy rhythms, which were often enveloped in a "sonic pollution" that could be very dark, serving as a direct reference for Lydon's new musical direction. "Sus rímicas grubis, rodeadas de esa pulución sonica, a veces muy oscura, son un claro referente para pil, la banda que formaría John Leidon tras Expistols."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: CAN ｜ La Banda que (posiblemente) Inspiró a tu banda preferida

podcast.title: Post-Sex Pistols Escape to Jamaica
podcast.body: After the Sex Pistols, Rotten reclaimed his birth name, John Lydon, and his first decision was to escape. He packed his bags and spent time in Jamaica, where he mingled with prominent dub artists. This Jamaican genre, based on echo, empty space, and heavy bass, would become one of the many genres defining post-punk. "Su primera decisión fue escapar, hizo las malitas y pasó una temporada en Jamaica, donde se codeó con los grandes totes del lab."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La traición que salvó al punk. PiL

podcast.title: Post-Sex Pistols Musical Freedom
podcast.body: After leaving the Sex Pistols, Johnny Lydon gained the freedom to pursue his personal musical interests, which included a strong admiration for the German avant-garde group Can. This freedom allowed him to indulge in new musical directions with Public Image Limited. "And once he was out of the sex pistols, he was free to indulge in his musical whims."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 3: Industrial

podcast.title: Potential Eyesight Deterioration
podcast.body: In addition to the permanent curvature of his spine and his distinctive stare, Johnny Lydon lives with the possibility that his eyesight will progressively deteriorate into nothingness due to the long-term effects of his childhood spinal meningitis. "He was also left with a permanent curvature of the spine and that stare and the possibility that his eyesight will deteriorate into nothingness."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians Battling Disease Part 2

podcast.title: Preference for Can Over Pink Floyd
podcast.body: John Lydon, the vocalist of Sex Pistols and PiL, famously "adored Can" but "hated Pink Floyd," underscoring a stark aesthetic division between the two bands in his view. "John Lidon, vocalista de Sex Pistol y Pill, adoraba can, pero daba Pink Floyd."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: CAN ｜ La Banda que (posiblemente) Inspiró a tu banda preferida

podcast.title: Profound Memory Loss and Identity Crisis
podcast.body: After being discharged from the hospital following his meningitis battle, Johnny Lydon suffered from severe memory loss that persisted for about four years, leaving him unable to recall his own name, his parents' names, or virtually anything from his past. He later reflected that this ordeal forced him to completely rebuild his identity, calling the meningitis "God's greatest gift" because it compelled him to discover who he truly was. "He couldn't remember his name or the name of his mom and dad."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians Battling Disease Part 2

podcast.title: Relationship Origin with Nora
podcast.body: Johnny met his wife Nora through her daughter, Ari. In the 1970s, Ari was in the punk band The Slits and moved in the same circles as the Sex Pistols, becoming friends with Johnny. "Johnny met Nora through Ari. Back in the 1970s, Ari was in a punk band called The Slits."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Star Kids ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Spinal Meningitis and Lasting Effects
podcast.body: Johnny Lydon contracted a severe case of spinal meningitis at the age of seven, an illness that left him with a permanent, intimidating stare and a lasting curvature of the spine. He spent an entire year at St. Anne's Hospital in London, enduring nausea, headaches, intermittent comas, hallucinations, and painful spinal taps, missing over a year of school. "It's the result of a terrible case of spinal men and gytus that he contracted when he was seven."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians Battling Disease Part 2

podcast.title: Stepfather to Ari
podcast.body: He is the stepfather to Nora's daughter, Ari. "He is, however, stepfather to Nora's daughter, Ari."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Star Kids ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Tired of Manipulation and Fakery
podcast.body: John Lydon was weary of Malcolm McLaren's manipulation to maintain the image of a destructive lunatic and tired of pretending to be a lout. In reality, he was a secret fan of English literature, passionate about Oscar Wilde, and a music lover with a very eclectic taste. "John y esta barto de que maglara el demanipular a mantener esa imagen del unático destructivo, esta barto de fingir que era un patán."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La traición que salvó al punk. PiL

podcast.title: Views on Disco Music (Metal Box Era)
podcast.body: During interviews for *Metal Box*, John Lydon began stating that the only contemporary music he liked was disco, a declaration considered absolute heresy by punk fans who still followed him. He argued that disco was functional, useful, and free from the "stupidities of conventional rock." "Laiton empezó a decirle a la entrevista que la única música contemporánea que le gustaba era la música disco."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La traición que salvó al punk. PiL

xref.title: Country Life Butter Commercial
xref.body: Johnny Rotten, also known as John Lydon, from The Sex Pistols, appeared in a commercial for Country Life butter. In the ad, he humorously justified his choice not based on British heritage or rural yearning, but simply because he believed it "tastes the best." "Johnny Leiden, Mr. Ratten from The Sex Pistols, for a brand of butter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 1

xref.title: John Lydon – Spinal Meningitis in Childhood Shaped His Personality and Punk Identity
xref.body: John Lydon (Johnny Rotten) contracted spinal meningitis as a child, which resulted in memory loss, spinal curvature, and the development of a markedly contrary and independent personality. These characteristics, forged by illness, were central to his becoming the iconic vocalist of the Sex Pistols. "Contracted spinal meningitis as a child, resulting in memory loss, a curvature of the spine, and a markedly contrary and independent personality."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Connections 3

xref.title: Johnny Rotten's Secret Wealth – Married to Publishing Heiress Worth ~£50 Million; Made Millions in UK Real Estate
xref.body: Despite assiduously maintaining his working-class punk image, John Lydon is married to Nora Forster, a German media and publishing heiress with an estimated net worth of approximately £50 million. They met during the Pistols' original run in the late 1970s when Lydon was about 22 and Forster was 36. Nora's daughter from a previous relationship was Ari Up, singer of The Slits — meaning Ari introduced her mother to Johnny. Additionally, unbeknownst to most punk fans, Lydon has made a considerable personal fortune by investing in the UK real estate market. "Johnny Rotten, punk by profession but secretly very, very comfortable."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 100 Weirdest Things in Alt-Rock: Part 9

xref.title: Roadie for Yes, Co-founded Public Image Ltd
xref.body: Keith Levene worked as a roadie for the progressive rock band Yes. After this, he went on to co-found Public Image Ltd with John Lydon (referred to as Johnny Leiden in the transcript). "Keith Levine was a roadie for yes before he hooked up with Johnny Leiden in public image limited."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
